system_overview: This specification models Huang's termination detection algorithm for distributed systems, proposed by Shing-Tsaan Huang in 1989. The algorithm solves the problem of determining when a distributed computation has completed -- that is, when all processes have become idle and no computational messages remain in transit. It uses a weight-splitting mechanism where the total weight across all processes and in-transit messages is conserved, allowing a designated controlling agent to detect global termination by observing that its own weight has returned to the initial total.
actors_and_components: The system consists of a finite set of processes interconnected in a fully meshed network, with one distinguished process designated as the leader (controlling agent). Each process can be in either an active or idle state. The leader initiates the computation and monitors for termination. Non-leader processes participate in the computation by sending and receiving messages, and report their weight back to the leader when they become idle.
state_variables: The system tracks three categories of state: (1) an activity flag for each process indicating whether it is currently active or idle, (2) a weight value for each process represented as a dyadic rational number (a fraction whose denominator is a power of two), and (3) a message queue for each process containing the weights of messages in transit to that process.
initial_state: The leader process starts in the active state with a weight of one. All other processes start in the idle state with a weight of zero. All message queues are initially empty.
actions: The system supports the following transitions: (1) Send message: An active process sends a computational message to any other process. It halves its current weight and attaches the halved weight to the message, which is appended to the recipient's message queue. (2) Receive message (non-leader): A non-leader process receives a message from its queue, becomes active, and adds the message's weight to its own weight. Messages may be received in any order. (3) Go idle (non-leader): An active non-leader process becomes idle. It sends its entire weight to the leader's message queue and resets its own weight to zero. (4) Leader goes idle: The active leader becomes idle without transferring any weight. (5) Leader receives message: The leader receives a weight message from its queue and adds the weight to its own, without changing its activity status.
safety_properties: The detection is safe: whenever the leader detects termination (it is idle and its weight equals one), actual termination has occurred -- meaning all processes are idle and all message queues are empty. Detection never produces a false positive. Additionally, a type correctness invariant ensures that the sum of all process weights and all in-transit message weights always equals one.
liveness_properties: The detection is live: if actual termination occurs (all processes are idle and all message queues are empty), the leader will eventually detect termination. The converse of detection leading to confirmed terminated state is also guaranteed.
model_bounds: The set of processes and the leader are declared as constants. For model checking, the denominator of weight fractions is constrained to not exceed 8, preventing the weight values from halving toward infinitely small values. A typical configuration uses 5 processes including the leader.
additional_assumptions: Weak fairness is assumed for the leader receiving messages, the leader going idle, and for each non-leader process receiving messages and going idle. The specification uses dyadic rationals (fractions with power-of-two denominators) to represent weights, ensuring exact arithmetic without rounding errors. The network is fully meshed, meaning any process can send a message to any other process. Messages may be received in any order (not necessarily FIFO). The algorithm assumes reliable message delivery -- it cannot detect termination if a message is lost in transit or if a process fails.
